subtitle: How many conversations share one wire, and how a call finds its way across a network.

fdm.body:
Wires are expensive. Digging a trench for every phone call would be absurd, so we make many conversations share one line. Multiplexing combines many signals onto one medium, and there are several ways to share.

FDM gives each signal its own frequency band (radio stations, cable TV) with guard bands between them, so neighbours don’t leak into each other. TDM gives each signal the whole channel for a short time slot in rotation, like speakers taking turns. Synchronous TDM wastes slots when a source is idle; statistical TDM allocates slots on demand. WDM is FDM for light: each colour carries a channel on one fibre.

Do a sum: a T1 line multiplexes 24 voice channels, each 64 kb/s, plus 8 kb/s framing. 24 × 64 = 1536 kb/s, and adding 8 kb/s framing gives 1544 kb/s. Why does FDM need guard bands? Real filters are not perfectly sharp.
keynotes: FDM gives each signal its own frequency band with guard bands between them; TDM gives each signal the whole channel for a short time slot in rotation.
Synchronous TDM wastes slots when a source is idle; statistical TDM allocates slots on demand; WDM is FDM for light.
A T1 line carries 24 × 64 = 1536 kb/s plus 8 kb/s framing, a total of 1544 kb/s.

dsl.body:
How can your home phone line also give you broadband? It was always copper wire that could carry far more than a voice. ADSL uses the copper pair in three frequency bands: voice (0–4 kHz), upstream and a much wider downstream band. It is asymmetric because home users download more than they upload.

The trick inside is discrete multitone: the band is split into 4 kHz sub-channels, each modulated with as many bits as its own signal-to-noise ratio allows. The further you live from the exchange, the slower it gets. What does the “A” in ADSL stand for? Asymmetric.
keynotes: ADSL uses the copper pair in three frequency bands: voice (0–4 kHz), upstream and a wider downstream band.
It is asymmetric because home users download more than they upload.
Discrete multitone splits the band into 4 kHz sub-channels, each carrying as many bits as its SNR allows; speed falls with distance from the exchange.

ss.body:
Here is a counter-intuitive trick: use far more bandwidth than you need, on purpose. Why? To hide in the noise and resist jamming. Spread spectrum comes in two flavours: FHSS hops the carrier among frequencies in a pseudo-random sequence, while DSSS multiplies each bit by a fast chipping code.

In CDMA every user has a different orthogonal code and all transmit at once on the same band; the receiver recovers one user by correlating with that user’s code, and the others average to zero. Take two users with orthogonal codes c₁ = (+1 +1 +1 +1) and c₂ = (+1 −1 +1 −1). User 1 sends bit +1, user 2 sends bit −1. The channel carries the sum c₁ − c₂ = (0, 2, 0, 2). User 1’s receiver correlates with c₁ and divides by 4: (0+2+0+2)/4 = +1. For user 2: correlate with c₂, (0·1 + 2·(−1) + 0·1 + 2·(−1))/4 = −1 ✓. Each receiver picks out its own user by correlating with that user’s code.
keynotes: Spread spectrum deliberately uses far more bandwidth than needed: FHSS hops the carrier among frequencies in a pseudo-random sequence; DSSS multiplies each bit by a fast chipping code.
In CDMA every user has a different orthogonal code and all transmit at once; the receiver correlates with that user’s code and the others average to zero.
With c₁ = (+1 +1 +1 +1) and c₂ = (+1 −1 +1 −1), the channel carries (0, 2, 0, 2), and correlating gives +1 for user 1 and −1 for user 2.

sw.body:
How does a call get from you to a friend across a whole network of links? There are three philosophies. Circuit switching reserves a path for the whole call (the telephone): guaranteed rate, set-up delay, idle capacity wasted. Message switching stores and forwards whole messages. Packet switching cuts data into packets routed separately: efficient for bursty traffic, with variable delay.

Packet switching comes in two flavours: datagram (each packet routed independently, and may arrive out of order) and virtual circuit (a path is set up first; packets follow it in order).

See the difference in numbers. Send a 1.5 MB file over 4 hops of 1 Mb/s each, ignoring propagation, as 1000 packets of 1500 B. Store-and-forward message switching retransmits the whole file at each hop: 4 × 12 s = 48 s. Packet switching pipelines: the first hop takes 12 s, then the last packet needs 3 more hop-times of 12 ms, so ≈ 12.04 s. Why is packet switching better for bursty data? Because capacity is shared, so nobody pays for idle silence.
keynotes: Circuit switching reserves a path for the whole call; message switching stores and forwards whole messages; packet switching routes packets separately.
Datagram routes each packet independently (may arrive out of order); virtual circuit sets up a path first and packets follow it in order.
A 1.5 MB file over 4 hops of 1 Mb/s takes 4 × 12 = 48 s by message switching but about 12.04 s by packet switching.

dev.body: What does a switch look like inside? A crossbar switch connects any input to any output with n² crosspoints, a grid of tiny gates. That is simple but gets huge, so multistage (Banyan/Clos) networks use fewer small switches at the price of possible blocking. A packet switch adds buffers to hold packets contending for the same output, like cars queuing at a junction. An n × n crossbar needs n² crosspoints.
keynotes: A crossbar switch connects any input to any output with n² crosspoints.
Multistage (Banyan/Clos) networks use fewer small switches at the price of possible blocking.
A packet switch adds buffers to hold packets contending for the same output.

summary.body:
One line each.

  • FDM splits frequency, TDM splits time, WDM splits colour, CDMA splits by code.
  • Circuit switching reserves; packet switching shares.
keynotes: FDM splits frequency, TDM splits time, WDM splits colour and CDMA splits by code.
Circuit switching reserves; packet switching shares.
